summary: Corruption of the Remaining Lifetime field in an IS-IS Link State PDU can go undetected, which may cause or worsen flooding storms and can also be used for denial of service. This proposed standard defines a backwards-compatible solution.

eli5.summary: If the clock on a note gets scribbled over, nobody notices and the note spreads wrongly. This adds a check so a damaged or tampered timer in routing messages gets caught.

questions: why is is-is lsp purged early
subtitle: A one-line change to how IS-IS routers store new LSPs, so a corrupted lifetime cannot trigger premature purges.

tldr.problem: The Remaining Lifetime field of an IS-IS LSP is excluded from the checksum and authentication hash, so corruption of it goes undetected. A value that is too small makes the LSP age out early, causing lost reachability and extra flooding.
tldr.mechanism: When a receiver stores a newer LSP whose Remaining Lifetime is below MaxAge, it sets the lifetime to MaxAge. A system other than the originator then never purges the LSP before it has been in the database for at least MaxAge.
tldr.outcome: The change is backwards compatible and also blunts a man-in-the-middle attack that shrinks the lifetime, even when cryptographic authentication is used. The cost is possibly keeping stale LSPs longer, which needs extra memory.

facts.label: New receive action
facts.value: Set lifetime to MaxAge if below MaxAge

today: RFC 7987 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2016. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Corrupted Lifetime Problem
sections.content:
An IS-IS Link State PDU (LSP), as defined in ISO 10589, carries a Remaining Lifetime field. The originator sets it from local configuration, and every system decrements it while the LSP sits in its LSP Database (LSPDB), so that all Intermediate Systems age the LSP out at about the same time.

Each LSP also has a checksum, calculated by the originator and not modifiable by other routers. The Remaining Lifetime is deliberately excluded from that checksum, and also from the hash when cryptographic authentication (RFC 5304 or RFC 5310) is used. If the field is corrupted during flooding, nobody can detect it.

If the lifetime becomes larger than intended, the impact is benign, because the originator refreshes the LSP before it ages out. If it becomes smaller, the LSP may be purged early, with two consequences: temporary loss of reachability to destinations described by that LSP, and unnecessary flooding when the originator regenerates it. If the value becomes very small and the cause persists, the cycle repeats and the impact can be significant.
sections.eli5: The timer on each routing note cannot be checked for tampering. A timer that is too long does no harm, but one that is too short makes a good note disappear and have to be sent again and again.

sections.title: The Fix: Raise Short Lifetimes to MaxAge
sections.content:
Normally only the originator updates or purges its LSP. ISO 10589 allows two cases where another system purges it: the LSP ages out (which should happen only if the originator is unreachable), or a Designated Intermediate System change on a LAN makes the old pseudonode LSPs unnecessary. In both cases purging is an optimization to remove stale entries, not required for correct operation.

A corrupted, too-small lifetime can make it look as if the originator failed to regenerate the LSP. To prevent this, the RFC adds one action to the rules for receiving an LSP that is newer than the local copy and has a nonzero Remaining Lifetime:

vi. If the Remaining Lifetime of the new LSP is less than MaxAge, it is set to MaxAge.

As a result, a system other than the originator never purges the LSP until it has existed in the database for at least MaxAge.

Handling of purged LSPs (zero Remaining Lifetime) is unchanged: a purge is still newer than a matching LSP with a nonzero lifetime. So the change does not cause LSPDB inconsistency among routers.
sections.eli5: When you pin up a new note, you give it a full-length timer no matter how short it arrived. Notes explicitly crossed out as thrown away are still handled the old way.

sections.title: Inconsistent MaxAge Values
sections.content:
ISO 10589 defines MaxAge as an architectural constant of 20 minutes (1200 seconds). In practice implementations let it be configured, usually to allow longer lifetimes and so reduce periodic regeneration of LSPs when the topology is stable (see RFC 3719). The originator's MaxAge can therefore be higher or lower than a receiver's.

If the originator's MaxAge is smaller than the receiver's, setting the lifetime to the receiver's MaxAge is safe. If the receiver's MaxAge is smaller, an LSP could still be purged prematurely. Implementors may therefore make the value to which the lifetime is set configurable. If so, the configured value MUST be greater than or equal to the locally configured MaxAge.
sections.eli5: Different routers may have different ideas of how long a full timer is. If yours is shorter than the sender's, you can choose to give notes a longer timer, but never a shorter one than your own.

sections.title: Reporting Corruption and Delayed Purging
sections.content:
Reporting a possibly corrupt lifetime helps find network problems. To limit false positives, an IS SHOULD treat a received LSP as possibly corrupt, and generate a CorruptRemainingLifetime event, only when all of these hold:

  • The LSP passed all acceptance tests in Section 7.3.15.1 of ISO 10589.
  • The LSP is newer than the local copy, including not being present in the LSPDB.
  • Its Remaining Lifetime is less than ZeroAgeLifetime.
  • The adjacency to the sending neighbor has been up for at least ZeroAgeLifetime.

The RFC notes this cannot catch every corruption, and not every event reported will be valid. As a diagnostic aid, an implementation MAY keep the lifetime value received when the LSP was added.

The extension can keep an LSP longer than its original lifetime, but only if the originator failed to refresh it, meaning it is unreachable. Neighbors then report the lost connectivity, and ISO 10589 says LSPs from an unreachable node are not used. So the only side effect is extra memory for the LSPDB.
sections.eli5: A router can raise a flag when a timer looks suspiciously short, but only when it is fairly sure, so it does not cry wolf. Keeping a dead router's old note a bit longer costs only a little space.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The rules do not change the ability to introduce corrupt LSPs. Authentication as defined in RFC 5304 and RFC 5310 prevents such LSPs being intentionally introduced.

A man-in-the-middle attack that changes an existing LSP's Remaining Lifetime to a small value can cause premature purges even when cryptographic authentication is in use, because the lifetime is outside the authenticated data. The mechanism in this document prevents such an attack from being effective.
sections.eli5: Even with a signature on the note, someone could still fiddle with its timer. Giving every pinned note a full timer takes the sting out of that trick.
